title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Normality Checks


library(e1071) # for skewness and kurtosis functions
skewness(bball$MP)

[1] -0.3155632

kurtosis(bball$MP)

[1] -0.8237927

shapiro.test(bball$MP)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  bball$MP
W = 0.97051, p-value = 3.561e-05

ks.test(bball$MP, "pnorm")


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  bball$MP
D = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two-sided


Rejecting the null is evidence against normality

Remember: This is evidence the data is non-normal. Sampling distribution still might be fine if \(N\) is large enough (hard to quantify with precision)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Confidence Interval
Sample mean is the point estimate of the population mean

Single value that will minimize our (squared) error to population mean

Confidence interval gives an interval estimate of the range in which the population mean lies
Definition of a confidence interval: range for which any random sample from the population will contain \(\mu\) with probability \(1 - \alpha\).

if \(\alpha = .05\), we have a 95% confidence interval.

Interpretation:

95% of intervals (across repeated samples) will contain \(\mu\)
If we treated any value inside the 95% confidence interval as the null, we could not reject it at \(\alpha = .05\)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text: 20 Confidence Intervals

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
General Procedure

Find the critical values of our reference distribution

Values on the distribution such that 2.5% is in the left tail and 2.5% in the right tail
These correspond to the “critical values” of the distribution

Transform these values back onto the scale of the original variable using the sample mean and standard error (\(\sigma_{\bar{x}}\))


Lower limit of \(\mu\): \(\bar{x} - \text{Critical Value} \times \sigma_{\bar{x}}\)
Upper limit of \(\mu\): \(\bar{x} + \text{Critical Value} \times \sigma_{\bar{x}}\)

This procedure corresponds to a two-tailed test

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
NBA Example

\(N = 44\)
\(\bar{x} = 14.5\)
\(\sigma = 6\)
\(\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{44}} = 0.90\)
\(df = N - 1 = 43\)

For a \(t\)-test, we can find the critical values as:


[1] 2.016692


Why p = .025?
We want 2.5% of the distribution in both the lowr and upper tails
\(95\% \text{CI} = 14.5 \pm 2.016 \times 0.90 = [12.69, 16.31]\)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text: NBA Example Visual

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
IMPORTANT
We are not claiming the plot on the right is the “true” sampling distribution

95% confidence intervals will vary sample to sample
The true parameter does not vary, it is a single fixed value
IF our assumptions hold, what we guarantee is that in 95% of samples, the 95% confidence interval (different in every sample) will contain the parameter 95% of the time

We can also say:

Any value inside the 95% confidence interval would be rejected if it were the null hypothesis
Any value outside the 95% confidence interval would be rejected if it were the null hypothesis

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Comparing Two Means
We’ve motivated the \(t\)-test by considering a case where

We have a hypothesis about a single population mean
We want to test whether our sample is consistent with that hypothesis

But what if we want to compare two means?

Changes in one group over time
Differences in paired observations
Differences between experiment and control groups
Differences in different existing groups

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Paired Samples \(t\)-Test

The one-sample \(t\)-test assumes independent observations
Some ways that independence can be violated:

Measuring the same person more than once
Measuring clusters of people

The paired (matched, repeated) samples \(t\)-test “builds in” a dependence structure:

Variable measured at two time points for the same \(N\) persons
Variable measured for pairs of subjects (younger/older siblings, husband/wife pairs)

For the paired samples \(t\)-test, all observations are paired
Take difference scores (\(D\)) for each pair of observations

A paired samples \(\boldsymbol t\)-test is equivalent to a one sample \(\boldsymbol t\)-test on difference scores

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Example
Original Study:

Berry, C. J., Shanks, D. R., & Henson, R. N. A. (2008). A single-system account of the relationship between priming, recognition, and fluency. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 34, 97-111.
Replication study link: https://osf.io/cbwgj/


Study phase:
Subjects were shown a series of words, and were instructed to click the mouse as soon as they could identify the word correctly
Test phase:
Subjects were shown another series of words and were asked to judge whether the word was “new” (not in the study phase) or “old” (already presented in the study phase)
\(N = 32\) subjects, 32 pairs of observations
\[H_0: \mu_{old} = \mu_{new}  \text{ or } \mu_{new} - \mu_{old} = 0\] \[H_a: \mu_{old} \neq \mu_{new} \text{ or } \mu_{new} - \mu_{old} \neq 0\]

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
The Nil Hypothesis
This is an example of the test of a nil hypothesis

There is no difference between old and new

Setting the null hypothesis to a difference of zero is so common it has it’s own term, but it is not strictly required.

You could test \(H_0: \mu_{new} - \mu_{old} = 5\) If you wanted!
It is just unusual that a difference of 5 would have any special significance

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Scope

Two groups where individual observations are matched across groups

Same individuals observed on two occasions/conditions
Pairs of individuals that are related in some way

Consider difference scores \(D_{1} = x_1 - y_2, \ldots, D_{N} = x_n - y_n\) for \(N\) pairs

Null (nil) Hypothesis:
\[H_0: \mu_{D} = \mu_0 = 0\] \[t_{\bar{D}} = \frac{\bar{D} - \mu_0}{s_{D} / \sqrt{N}}\]
Reference distribution:
\[t \text{ with } df = N-1\]

\(N\) is the number of pairs

text:
95% Confidence Interval
Just like the one sample case, we can calculate a 95% confidence interval as
\[95\% \text{ CI} = \bar{D} \pm \text{Critical Value} \times S_{\bar{D}}\]
First we need to know our critical value (\(t_{crit}\))

t_crit <- qt(p = .025, df = 31, lower.tail = FALSE)

Then we plug into our formula

D_bar - t_crit * SE

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
APA Writeup
For every participant, priming was calculated as the mean response time for new items minus the mean response time for old items. Using \(\alpha = .05\), priming was significantly greater than zero overall, \(t(31) = 10.40, p < .001\), indicating that the old items were identified more quickly at test than new items (\(\bar{D} = 108.9\rm{ms, 95\%}\) \(\rm{CI = [87.5, 130.2]).}\)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Independent Groups
In many cases, we may want to test whether two independently sampled groups have the same population mean

Randomized experiments in which different groups get different treatments

Does a new experimental drug lead to better patient outcomes than a control?

Differences in pre-existing groups

Do people with PhDs in psychology have higher average career earnings than people who do not?


\[H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\] \[H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0\]
Now we must consider the sampling distribution of the means of two separate (unpaired) groups: \(\bar{x_1} - \bar{x_2}\)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Sampling Differences
If both \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are normally distributed:

The sampling distribution of mean differences will be normal

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
A New Assumption
An independent sample \(t\)-test has the same assumptions we’ve already established

Normality of sampling distribution
Indepence of observations
No outliers
Random sampling

Plus one new one:

Homogeneity of Variance: Even if the populations have different means, they have the same variance (SD) around those means
We assume in the population both groups have the same variance: \(\sigma^2_1 = \sigma^2_2\)

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Pooled Variance

Sample variances will differ (even if homogeneity holds) just due to sampling variation. To get the best estimate of the shared population variance, we need to pool (average) them
Pooled variance (\(s^2_p\)): estimate of the common population variance
\[s^2_p = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s^2_1 + (n_2 - 1)s^2_2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]

Weighted average of the two sample variances
\(n_1\): sample size for group 1 (lower-case \(n\) for group sample size)
\(n_2\): sample size for group 2
\(s^2_1\): sample variance for group 1
\(s^2_2\): sample variance for group 2

\(s_p = \sqrt{s^2_p}\) is the pooled standard deviation

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Homogeneity Example
Homogeneity of Variance means two populations have the same variance, even if they have different means:
\[\text{Population}_1 \sim \text{Normal}(10, 10) \ \ \text{Population}_2 \sim \text{Normal}(5, 10)\]

\(\mu_1 = 10 \neq \mu_2 = 5\)
\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma = 10\)

Let’s simulate 10,000 samples of \(N = 5\) from each population and calculate \(s_1\), \(s_2\), and \(s_p\). Which do you think will be closest to \(\sigma = 10\)?

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Simulated Homogeneity

mu1 <- 10
mu2 <- 5
sigma1 <- sigma2 <- 10
N <- 5
samples <- 10000
## Create empty data frame to save results
sd_estimates <- data.frame(s1 = rep(NA, samples),
                           s2 = rep(NA, samples),
                           sp = rep(NA, samples))
set.seed(4441)
for(i in 1:samples){
  ## Draw samples
  sample1 <- rnorm(n = N, mean = mu1, sd = sigma1)
  sample2 <- rnorm(n = N, mean = mu2, sd = sigma2)
  
  ## Calculate SDs
  s1 <- sd(sample1)
  s2 <- sd(sample2)
  s2p <- ((N - 1) * s1^2 + (N - 1) * s2^2)/(N + N - 2) # pooled variance
  sp <- sqrt(s2p) # pooled sd
  
  ## Save SDs
  sd_estimates$s1[i] <- s1
  sd_estimates$s2[i] <- s2
  sd_estimates$sp[i] <- sp
}

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Visualized Estimates


\(s_p\) is doing a better job of estimating \(\sigma\) than either \(s_1\) or \(s_2\) because the sample size used to calculate it is twice as large.

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Test Statistic
\[t_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 }{s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]
Where
\[s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{s_p^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_p^2}{n_2}}\]
Is our pooled standard error

Takes into account differences in group sample sizes

Reference distribution:
\[t \text{ with } df = n_1 + n_2 -2\]

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Example
Original Study:

McCrea, S. M. (2008). Self-handicapping, excuse making, and counterfactual thinking: Consequences for self-esteem and future motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2, 274-292.


Replication study link: https://osf.io/2kjgz
Step 1: Subject took a math exam and were told that they scored in the 35th percentile of university students
Step 2: Subjects saw statements supposedly written by previous participants

Self-handicap group: half of statements indicated that more practice would have improved their performance, half of statements were neutral
Control group: all statements were neutral

Step 3: Subjects took a second surprise math exam

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Research Question
Were scores different on the second exam between the self-handicap and control groups?
\(n_{\text{self-handicap}} = 32\), \(n_{\text{control}} = 29\)
\[H_0: \mu_{self-handicap} = \mu_{control}\] \[H_a: \mu_{self-handicap} \neq \mu_{control}\]
or
\[H_0: \mu_{self-handicap} - \mu_{control} = 0\] \[H_a: \mu_{self-handicap} - \mu_{control} \neq 0\]

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Reading in Data
Variables of interest

Cond is experimental condition

I’m going to recode this variable to have descriptive names first

percent is the percent of items corrrect on the second test


dat <- read.csv("../../data/McCrea.csv") |> 
  mutate(Cond = recode(as_factor(Cond), 
                       "1" = "self-handicap", 
                       "2" = "control"))

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Calculating Statistics

(means <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(percent)))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Cond           mean
  <fct>         <dbl>
1 self-handicap 0.466
2 control       0.583

(sds <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(sd = sd(percent)))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Cond             sd
  <fct>         <dbl>
1 self-handicap 0.169
2 control       0.224

(ns <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(n = n()))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Cond              n
  <fct>         <int>
1 self-handicap    32
2 control          29

## extract x_bar1, x_bar2, s1, s2, n1, and n2
x_bar1 <- means$mean[1]
x_bar2 <- means$mean[2]
s1 <- sds$sd[1]
s2 <- sds$sd[2]
n1 <- ns$n[1]
n2 <- ns$n[2]

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
More Stats
Calculate the pooled variance and then SD:

(s2p <- ((n1 - 1) * s1^2 + (n2 - 1) * s2^2)/(n1 + n2 - 2))

[1] 0.03869851

(sp <- sqrt(s2p))

[1] 0.1967194


Calculate the standard error \(\sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}\):

(SE <- sp * sqrt((1/n1) + (1/n2)))

[1] 0.0504357


Calculate the \(t_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}\)-statistic:

(t_xbar1_xbar2 <- (x_bar1 - x_bar2)/SE)

[1] -2.325462


Calculate \(p\)-value (use absolute value of \(t_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}\))

pt(abs(t_xbar1_xbar2), df = n1 + n2 - 2, lower.tail = FALSE) * 2

[1] 0.0235052

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Confidence Interval
The confidence interval follows the same formula we have seen
\[\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \pm \text{Critical Value} \times \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}\]
Critical value:

(t_crit <- qt(.025, df = n1 + n2 - 2, lower.tail = FALSE))

[1] 2.000995


Confidence Interval:

x_bar1 - x_bar2 - t_crit * SE

[1] -0.2182079

x_bar1 - x_bar2 + t_crit * SE

[1] -0.01636472

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Using Built in R
For an independent sample \(t\)-test in R we can use the formula syntax

Outcome (dependent) variable first
~ next
Grouping (independent) variable last
For standard \(t\)-test, we specify var.equal = TRUE


t.test(percent ~ Cond, data = dat, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  percent by Cond
t = -2.3255, df = 59, p-value = 0.02351
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group self-handicap and group control is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.21820793 -0.01636472
sample estimates:
mean in group self-handicap       mean in group control 
                  0.4661788                   0.5834651

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Behrens-Fisher Problem

If all assumptions hold, then
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \sim t(n_1 + n_2 - 2)\]

\(s^2_p\) only makes sense to compute if \(\sigma^2_1 = \sigma^2_2\)
What if the homogeneity assumption is not tenable (populations have different variances)?

If we instead compute:
\[t^\prime = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{s^2_2}{n_2}}} \,\,\sim \,\,??\]
Problem: \(t^\prime\) follows a slightly different distribution

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
Welch-Satterthwaite Correction
Welch-Satterthwaite corrected \(t\)-test:
Test statistic (same as before):
\[t(df) = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}}\]
Standard error (does not pool variances):
\[s_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{s^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{s^2_2}{n_2}}\]
Degrees of freedom (adjust downwards, can be fractional:
\[df = \frac{\left(\frac{s^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{s^2_2}{n_2}\right)^2}{\left(\frac{s^2_1}{n_1}\right)^2 / (n_1 - 1) + \left(\frac{s^2_2}{n_2}\right)^2 / (n_2 - 1)}\]

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
In R
The Welch-Satterthwaite correction is the default in R

Virtually no “cost” if homogeneity of variance happens to hold
Helps if homogeneity of variance does not hold
Just use this version in practice!


t.test(percent ~ Cond, data = dat)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  percent by Cond
t = -2.2938, df = 51.895, p-value = 0.02588
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group self-handicap and group control is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.21989383 -0.01467881
sample estimates:
mean in group self-handicap       mean in group control 
                  0.4661788                   0.5834651

title: Lecture 9: More You Can Do with t
text:
APA Writeup
A two-tailed Welch-Satterthwaite \(t\)-test with \(\alpha = .05\) indicated a significant difference between conditions, \(t(51.9) = -2.29, p = .026\). Participants in the self-handicap condition correctly answered a lower percentage of items (\(N = 32, M = .47, SD = .17\)) than participants in the control condition (\(N = 29, M = .58, SD = .22\)), 95% CI of the difference \(= [0.01, 0.22]\).

title: Data Manipulation and Simulation
text:
Simulation Example: CLT
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that the sampling distribution of the mean of any distribution with finite mean and variance will converge to be normal with increasing sample size.

○ Imagine: take a sample of \(N\) observations from the population, calculate some statistics (e.g., the mean), and toss them back.


○ Repeat a whole bunch of times


○ Sampling distribution: the distribution of those calculated statistics (e.g., means)

Let’s say we’re not so sure, and we want to test this out with different distributions and sample sizes \(N\).

title: Data Manipulation and Simulation
text:
Simulation Example: CLT
Before simulating, define your goals / questions.


Questions
Does the sampling distribution of the mean really converge to normal for wonky asymmetrical distributions like the \(\chi^2\) distribution?
At what sample sizes does this fail?

Goals
See if the distribution of means from repeatedly sampling data looks normal

○ Does this change with different original distributions from which the data is drawn?


○ Does this change with sample size?

title: Data Manipulation and Simulation
text:
Simulation Example: CLT
Then, sketch out a plan. Try to build things up step-by-step, not all at once.

Start with data sampled from a normal distribution. Generate one sample of data, take its mean.
Repeat this process multiple times, generating replications of data samples and sample means.
Visualize both: the original distribution of the data (sample distribution), the distribution of the the samples’ means (sampling distribution).
Incorporate different distributions.
Incorporate different sample sizes.

title: Data Manipulation and Simulation
text:
Simulation Example: CLT

Start with data sampled from a normal distribution. Generate one sample of data, take its mean.



rnorm(x, mean, sd) where x is the number of samples

tibble()


A tibble() is just like a dataframe, but better. The best part is its printing—tibble()s will never crowd your screen by trying to show every single value of a dataframe. Also, they work better with making tibbles in tibbles in tibbles… More on tibbles here.

title: Data Manipulation and Simulation
text:
Let Us Review…
What are the tidy principles?

Three rules to a tidy dataset


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable.
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation.
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value.

Long vs. Wide Data
Long: each observation is a row (tidy)

○ Observation does not necessarily mean “person”


○ Can be within-person measurements over time

Wide: columns might represent different “values” of a variables

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
text:
Chi-Squared (\(\chi^2\)) Test
Testing inferences about proportions
○ Involve categorical variables
Comparing observed frequencies (counts) to some expected (null hypothesis) frequencies
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit: expected frequencies are set by researcher (e.g., null hypothesis is equal frequencies across all groups)
\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence: expected frequencies are those implied by independence

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
text:
Chi-Squared (\(\chi^2\)) Test
Instead of a continuous variable, our outcome is a count


Continuous

Height
Petal length
Test score


Counts

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit: Hypotheses
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit: Hypotheses
\(H_0\): Observed data match the expected frequencies for the population
\(H_1\): Observed data do not match the expected frequencies for the population
○ Observed frequency is significantly different than expected

\(H_0\): \(\pi_j = \pi_{j_0}\) for all categories \(j\) (i.e., difference for all categories is 0), where
\(\pi_j\) = observed proportion
\(\pi_{j_0}\) = expected proportion
\(H_1\): \(\pi_j \neq \pi_{j_0}\) for any category \(j\)

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]
where
\(O_j\) = observed frequency
\(N\) = total sample size
\(E_j\) = expected frequency
\(j\) = individual category out of \(J\) total categories
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each group.

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
\(\text{df} = J - 1\), where
\(J\) = number of categories
Use to identify critical \(\chi^2\) value from \(\chi^2\) table, R, etc.
For \(\chi^2\), as \(\text{df}\) increases, so does the critical-\(\chi^2\) value (at same \(\alpha\))
Only ever a one-tailed test! For the upper end of the distribution.

Do the observed frequencies of a categorical variable differ from what expected via properties of independence?

Expected frequencies calculated from the marginal totals of the contingency table
○ Expected values determined from data

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence: Hypotheses
\(H_0\): Categorical Variable 1 and Categorical Variable 2 are independent (i.e., have no association)
\(H_1\): Categorical Variable 1 and Categorical Variable 2 are not independent (i.e., have some association)
○ Do expected frequencies match those expected via independence?

Mathematically the same as before:
\(H_0\): \(\pi_j = \pi_{j_0}\) for all categories \(j\); difference for all categories is 0, where
\(\pi_j\) = observed proportion
\(\pi_{j_0}\) = expected proportion
\(H_1\): \(\pi_j \neq \pi_{j_0}\) for any category \(j\)


Just changing the expected frequencies

title: Simulations and Chi-Squared Tests
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence Generally
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]
Basically identical formula to calculate the \(\chi^2\).
The difference is that our expected frequencies \(E_j\) are derived from the data. Just like before, we calculate the difference from each cell, but now we have two categories that make up the cell.
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each cell.

title: Lab 03 Activity Key
text:
Simulation

3) Extend or modify the data simulation shown in class in some way. Feel free to choose something interesting to you, but some possible ideas are: adding an additional condition, modifying an existing condition, replacing some distributions with different ones, comparing distributions with different parameters (e.g., comparing different means, SDs, degrees of freedom, etc. within a distribution). For this extension, write 1–2 questions or goals below.

Compare how the CLT behaves with \(\chi^2\) tests of different degrees of freedom.



4) Next, make your plan. This can be brief, but sketch out the steps you will take to program this. If your extension involves varying some parameters, distribution, etc., specify the different levels it will take (e.g., testing a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom 1, 2, 3, and 4).
Replace existing distributions with \(chi^2\) distributions of varying degrees of freedom, specifically df = 1, 2, 3, and 4.


5) Make your modifications to the simulation and show the results! Please include results for both the sample and sampling distributions.

n_reps <- 1000
sample_size <- c(3, 10, 30, 100)
total_n <- sum(n_reps * sample_size)

sim_data <- tibble(
  n_reps = n_reps,
  sample_size = sample_size
) |>
  uncount(n_reps, .id = "rep") |>
  uncount(sample_size, .id = "index", .remove = F) |>
  mutate(
    draw_chisq_1 = rchisq(total_n, df = 1),

title: Lab 03 Activity Key
text:
Chi-Squared Test of Proportions

3) Download and relocate the leaves.csv file to your folder for this class. Read in the file and display the first few rows of the data. This dataset contains the color (green, red, orange, or brown) and whether a not a leaf had fallen from its tree for 1,000 leaves (Note: this is a simulated dataset). Use mutate() to change the color variable into an factor variable ordered by the leaf changing process (green -> red -> orange -> brown) first.

leaves <- read.csv(here::here("lab", "data", "leaves.csv")) |>
  mutate(color = factor(color, levels = c("green", "red", "orange", "brown")))



4a) You are a tree researcher, and you would like to better understand leaves changing color in the fall. You’ve recorded the color of 1000 leaves, and you’d like to test if there is a difference in the frequency of the colors of the leaves. You plan to conduct a Chi-Squared Test of Proportions on the frequency of different color leaves you’ve observed in your dataset. First, what are the null and alternative hypotheses for this test?
\(H_0\): The frequency of leaves of each color is the same in the population.
\(H_A\): The frequency of leaves of each color is not the same in the population.


4b) What is the expected frequency for leaves of each color?
250 each.


4c) What is your chi-square degrees of freedom and cutoff value?

qchisq(.95, 3)

[1] 7.814728


\(\text{df} = 4 - 1 = 3\), cutoff = 7.815.


4d) What are the observed frequencies of each color?

table(leaves$color)


 green    red orange  brown 
   109    297    499     95 




4e) What is the observed chi-squared statistic?

chisq.test(c(94, 104, 513, 289))


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  c(94, 104, 513, 289)
X-squared = 465.37, df = 3, p-value < 2.2e-16




4f) Provide a brief interpretation of these results.
We reject the null in favor of the alternative that there is a difference among the frequencies of these leaf colors in the population.


4g) Create a barplot that displays the frequencies of each leaf color.

leaves |>

  geom_bar()

\(H_0\): Leaf color and whether or not the leaf had fallen have no association.
\(H_A\): Leaf color and whether or not the leaf had fallen have some association.


5b) What are the observed frequencies of each color given whether or not they had fallen?

table(leaves$color, leaves$fallen)

            n = n()) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = fallen, values_from = n) |>
  select(-color) |>

Adding Math Equations
In Quarto, we can use LaTeX (pronounced “lah-tech” or “lay-tech”) to render nice-looking math symbols and equations
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i \qquad \quad \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{N} \qquad \quad s^2 = \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N-1}
\]
For inline LaTeX (e.g., \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2\)), wrap the equation in single dollar signs $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$.
For LaTeX on its own line, like above, wrap the equation in double dollar signs $$a^2 = b^2 + c^2$$
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\]

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Probability and Statistics




Probability tells us how data are randomly generated based on some underlying facts about a population.

Statistics are how we infer underlying facts about a population from a finite set of observed data (sample).

This course will begin and end with statistics, with many detours to probability along the way

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Terminology
The difference between statistics and probability is in what is known or held constant

In probability parameters are assumed to be known

Parameter: A quantity that describes (a property of) an entire population, traditionally denoted with Greek letter (\(\sigma\), \(\mu\), \(\beta\))

In statistics data are assumed to be known

What IS/ARE data? (Singular: datum)

Distinct pieces of observed information
Statistic: Quantity calculated from a finite amount of data to estimate a parameter, traditionally denoted with English letter (\(s\), \(M\), \(b\))

We often arrange data into rectangular datasets

Measurement Scales

Stevens (1946) classified variables as being measured on one of four scales:

Nominal: Variables with discrete categories
Ordinal: Variables with ordering or ranking, distances between scale points are not equal
Interval: Distances between scale points are equal (zero has no special meaning)


Alternatively: 


Ratio: Distances between scale points are equal (zero has a special meaning, usually the absence of the trait)

Median: Score that corresponds to the point at or below which 50% of scores fall (order data first)

Also known as the 50\(^{\text{th}}\) percentile

Mean: \(\bar{x} = \sum x / N\). Anyone want to try and break down this notation? It’s important!

The trimmed mean is a robust statistic that reduces the two disadvantages of the mean

Sensitivity to asymmetric distributions
Sensitivity to extreme values

5% trimmed mean is the mean of the data that discards the lowest 5% and the highest 5% of values in the original data
The mode is the value with the highest frequency

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Range and IQR

Variability measures how spread out the data are

Range: = maximum value - minimum value

Highly sensitive to extreme values
Does not use all of the information in the data

Interquartile Range (IQR) = \(75^\text{th}\) percentile - \(25^\text{th}\) percentile

\(25^\text{th}\) percentile = \(1^\text{st}\) quartile (1Q)
\(75^\text{th}\) percentile = \(3^\text{rd}\) quartile (3Q)
Less sensitive to extreme values
Does not use all of the information in the data

Some variables are commonly known to be asymmetric with extreme values. Example: household income
For these variables, best to report median + IQR
Example: median annual household income in Manhattan (as of 2014) = $66,739, IQR = $24,567

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Variance and SD

Variance (sample: \(s^2\), population: \(\sigma^2\)):
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{N-1}\,\,\,\,\, \sigma^2 = \frac{\sum(x - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\((x - \bar{x})\): deviation scores (deviation from mean)
\((x - \bar{x})^2\): square deviation scores to make them positive
\(\frac{\sum}{N-1}\): average
\((N-1)\) are degrees of freedom used in the sample calculation

Standard Deviation (sample: \(SD\) or \(s\), population: \(\sigma\))

Square root of the variance
Variance is in squared units, SD is in the units of the original variable

Degrees of freedom (\(df\)) are the number of elements in a statistic’s calculation that are free to vary

For the variance calculation, we lose 1 \(df\) by calculating the sample mean

Let’s consider the following set of numbers [1, 2, \(x\)]. What is \(x\)?
What if I told you that the mean of these three numbers was \(\bar{x} = 2\). Now what is \(x\)?

Degrees of Freedom Simulated

Sometimes when you want to prove a concept to yourself, it helps to simulate it.
In the following slides I:

Set the population mean \(\mu = 0\)
Set the population variance \(\sigma^2 = 10\)
Generated sets of \(N = 5\) random numbers using these parameters
Calculated the variance of each sample using each of the following formulas

\(\frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{N}\)
\(\frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{N - 1}\)

Repeated the process 100,000 times
Plotted distribution of \(s^2\) values to compare how well the sample statistics from these two formulas reproduced the known variance parameter \(\sigma^2 = 10\)

Our goal is to have \(s^2\) equal to the \(\sigma^2\) on average

Mean and Variance of Discrete Data
Consider the binary variable we created “Was the player drafted or not?”

What do the mean and variance mean?

Mean of a binary variable \(p\)

\(p\) is the proportion in category “1”
In this example, \(p\) is the proportion players who were drafted

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Skewness
Skewness is the degree of asymmetry in a variable
\[\text{Skew} = \frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^3 / N}{[\sum(x - \bar{x})^2 / N]^{3/2}}\]

Skew = 0 indicates a symmetric distribution
Negative or left skew: long left tail
Positive or right skew: long right tail

Direction of skewness is where the long tail is

Higher magnitude of skew: more asymmetric variable

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text: Skewness

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Kurtosis
Kurtosis is the degree of peakedness in the variable
\[\text{Kurtosis} = \left(\frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^4}{N}\right) \bigg/ \left(\frac{\sum(x - \bar{x}^2)}{N}\right)^2 - 3\]

Kurtosis = 0: mesokurtic
Normal distribution is mesokurtic
Negative kurtosis: platykurtic (lighter tails)
Positive kurtosis: leptokurtic (heavier tails)

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text: Kurtosis

title: Lecture 2: Exploring Data
text:
Moments of Distributions
Why are skewness and kurtosis defined as they are?








Metric
Population Expression
Sample Statistic




Mean(Center)
\(\mu = E(X)\)
\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{N}\)


Variance(Deviation)
\(\sigma^{2} = E[(X-\mu)^{2}]\)
\(s^{2} = \frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2}}{N-1}\)


Skewness(Asymmetry)
\(E[(X-\mu)^{3}]\)
\(\frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^{3}/N}{\left[\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2}/N\right]^{3/2}}\)


Kurtosis(Peakedness)
\(E[(X-\mu)^{4}]\)
\(\frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^{4}/N}{\left[\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2}/N\right]^{2}} - 3\)

Much of statistics is about using numerical summaries of data, since what we’re often ultimately interested in is estimating parameters.
But interpreting numbers is hard!
Next time we will look at another way of interpreting data….

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Binomials

We can also use the binomial distribution to consider cumulative outcomes by summing the probabilities of each outcome within a cumulative range.
For example, the probability that we would draw fewer than three (exactly zero, exactly one, or exactly two) pineapples in bags of 10 bears is:
\[P(\text{fewer than three pinapples}) = \frac{10!}{0!(10-0)!}.2^0 (1-.2)^{10-0} +\] \[\frac{10!}{1!(10-1)!}.2^1 (1-.2)^{10-1} + \frac{10!}{2!(10-2)!}.2^2 (1-.2)^{10-2} = .68\]
And we can get the complement of this cumulative probability by just subtracting it from 1. The probability we would draw at least three pineapples is
\[P(\text{at least three pinapples}) = 1 - P(\text{fewer than three pinapples}) =\] \[1 - .68 = .32\]

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#what-is-bayesian-inference
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#what-is-bayesian-inference
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
What is Bayesian Inference
NHST is a decision rule framework for how we make a categorical choice: do we decide to reject the null hypothesis?

Bayesian inference is also a kind of decision rule, but it is not discrete, it is continuous.
Way of defining how we can use new data to updating our existing beliefs about what a population parameter is likely to be.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
Let’s imagine we have a coin, we want to determine the true proportion of times that the coin will land on heads (vs. tails).

We will call the coin’s true proportion of landing on heads (which is unknown) \(\pi\).
We then flip the coin 10 times, and observe 7 heads and 3 tails, which is our “data,” which we will call \(\boldsymbol{D}\).

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
\[P(\theta|D) = \frac{P(D|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(D)}\]

\(P(\pi)\) - our prior belief about the proportion of times the coin will lands heads

Notice: The true \(\pi\) is unknown. This is a statement about our confidence it might take on certain values. So we might think it is very likely 50%, but there is some chance it is not, and is an unfair coin

\(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\) - The likelihood of observing 7 heads and 3 tails, given the (unknown) true \(\pi\).
\(P(\boldsymbol{D})\) - The probability of observing 7 heads and 3 tails unconditionally

One way to define this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\)
Really we typically need calculus for this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta\)

\(P(\theta | \boldsymbol{D})\) - the posterior belief about the proportion of times the coin will land on heads, incorporating both the prior and the data.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#probabilities-of-probabilities
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#probabilities-of-probabilities
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Probabilities of Probabilities
Notice that our prior is a probability statement about not about how likely the coin is to land on heads, but our confidence in the true proportion of times the coin will land on heads \(\pi\). If we are very confident, our prior might look something like this.

This plot suggests we think it’s very likely the coin is fair, though there’s some possibiliy is is weighted more heavily towards heads or tails.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#frequentists-hate-him
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#frequentists-hate-him
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Frequentists HATE him
This is the part frequentists object to. For a frequentist:

Only “random variables” can be represented by a probability distribution
The true proportion of heads is not a random variable
It is a single number, a cold hard fact, just one that we don’t know

For a Bayesian

Probability refers to what is known, not just what is true or not true

Bayseians treat probability as a psychological phenomenon
Frequentists treat probability as a metaphysical phenomenon

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#two-takes-on-probability
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#two-takes-on-probability
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Two Takes on Probability



Frequentists: Parameters are facts about the world that are constant and can only actually be single values. The only things that are random are the data. We can’t reverse the probability arrow population \(\rightarrow\) sample
Bayesians: The only constants we can actually know are the facts we observe (data). Based on our limited knowledge, we need to a way to quantify how likely different possible parameters are. Probability is a general use language we use to describe the likelihood of different unknowns (parameters) based on our knowledge (data)

Which philosophical position do you take?

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#posterior-belief
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Posterior Belief

If we have a strong prior belief, seeing 7 heads and 3 tails should make us think if our coin happens to be unfair, it’s more likely to be weighted towards heads than tails. But seven heads and three tails aren’t that surprising for a fair coin, so our belief won’t change that much.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#a-different-prior
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#a-different-prior
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
A Different Prior

What if an alien came to earth with no knowledge about how coins worked? They might have no idea the true proportion of times most coins land on heads, and think all possible values of \(\pi\) are equally likely

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#aliens-posterior-belief
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#aliens-posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Alien’s Posterior Belief

In this case, the data might be quite persuasive! After seeing 7 heads and 3 tails, the alien might be fairly convinced that the coin was weighted towards heads.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
In practice, priors are specified as probability distributions.
For example, if I am very confident the coin is likely to be fair, my prior might be a normal distribution with \(\mu = 0.5\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\).

\(\mu = 0.5\) means I think the true proportion of heads is most likely to be \(0.5\),
\(\sigma = 0.1\) means that in my mind, I am around 68% certain that the true proportion is between \(0.4\) and \(0.6\)

Because 68% of the values in a normal distribution are within 1 SD of the mean

Likewise, I am around 98% certain the true proportion is between \(0.3\) and \(0.7\)

Because 98% of the values in a normal distribution are within 2 SD of the mean

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
This prior would technically be improper. Can anyone see why?
A normal distribution can have values from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\), but a proportion can only be between 0 and 1
This is one of the reasons Bayesian Statsitics is more complex to learn.
You can use improper priors, but in general, proper priors are going to allow us to do more and more interesting things.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-incorportate-data
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#how-to-incorportate-data
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Incorportate Data
How does data move us from prior to posterior?
Through the likelihood function
\[P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)P(\pi)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\pi)\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#likelihood-function-of-our-data
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#likelihood-function-of-our-data
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text: Likelihood Function of our Data

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#maximum-likelihood
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#maximum-likelihood
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Maximum Likelihood
Recall: To find the maximum likelihood, we find the highest point on the hill

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#map-estimation
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#map-estimation
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MAP Estimation
One approach to Bayesian estimation is very similar to Maximum Likelihood. It is known as Maximum A Posteriori estimation (MAP). Under MAP, we aren’t necessarily interested in the actual probability distribution \(P(\pi |\boldsymbol{D})\), just the value of \(\pi\) that maximizes this function.
Notice what this allows us to do with Bayes’ rule:
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta}\]
Because we don’t care about the equality, only the maximum point, we can drop out the denominator, and instead say
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) \propto P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\]
Where \(\propto\) means “is proportional to”.
This is a common approach when the primary goal is making predictions, rather than making a confidence statement about parameter values.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#general-form
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#general-form
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Form
The coin flip was a motivating example, but not very practice. Our general version of Bayes’ rule is:
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})\)

This allows us to consider our confidence in multiple parameters simultaneously, represented generically as \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mccrea-revisited
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mccrea-revisited
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
McCrea Revisited
Original Study:

McCrea, S. M. (2008). Self-handicapping, excuse making, and counterfactual thinking: Consequences for self-esteem and future motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2, 274-292.


Replication study link: https://osf.io/2kjgz
Step 1: Subject took a math exam and were told that they scored in the 35th percentile of university students
Step 2: Subjects saw statements supposedly written by previous participants

Self-handicap group: half of statements indicated that more practice would have improved their performance, half of statements were neutral
Control group: all statements were neutral

Step 3: Subjects took a second surprise math exam

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#general-linear-model
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#general-linear-model
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Linear Model
For example, recall that we can rewrite a \(t\)-test in the form of a simple linear model
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Group}_i + \epsilon_i\]
Our parameter space here is \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)

\(\beta_0 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 0\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 1\)
\(\sigma_\epsilon =\) shared standard deviation for each group (residual SD)

We want to estimate Bayes’ rule without losing the denominator, complex integral and all
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})  = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}}\]

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a simulation-based procedure for determining the goint of posterior distribution of all parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) when it’s too complicated to figure out numerically.
There are many different MCMC based algorithms. In a very general/intuitive sense, the way MCMC works is as follows:

We draw random values from \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) based on our prior, and check how well those values “fit” our likelihood
If the fit is not good enough we (might) throw away that draw (probabilistically) and make another one
If it is good enough, we keep it, and update our parameter estimates based on this value
We repeat this process many times, until we have a large “synthetic sample” of values that represent the combination of our prior and the likelihood
We use the simulated values that we kept as a representation of the posterior distribution \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-slightly-more-detail
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-slightly-more-detail
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: Slightly More Detail
In our example, where \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)
Step 1: Choose starting values for each parameter as draws from their prior distributions. Call them \(\beta_{0_1}\), \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).
Step 2: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{0}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{0_2}\).
Step 3: Determine whether \(\beta_{0_1}\) or \(\beta_{0_2}\) is at a higher point on the likelihood function (data given parameters), with \(\beta_{1}\) assumed to be \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) assumed to be \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).

That is: Check whether \(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-slightly-more-detail-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-slightly-more-detail-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: Slightly More Detail
Step 4: If

\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\), keep the proposed value \(\beta_{0_2}\) for sure.
\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) < \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\) only keep \(\beta_{0_2}\) with probability based on the ratio \(\frac{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1}; \boldsymbol{D})}{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})}\)

Step 5: if \(\beta_{0_2}\) was kept, save it as a viable element of the posterior distribution of \(\beta_{0}\). Otherwise, throw it away.
Step 6: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{1}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{1_2}\).
Step 7: Repeat steps 3-5, but for \(\beta_{1_2}\) rather than \(\beta_{0_2}\), and using \(\beta_{0_2}\) if it was accepted as a proposal, and \(\beta_{0_1}\) if it was not.
Step 8: Repeat steps 3-5 for \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) using \(\beta_{0_2}\) and \(\beta_{1_2}\) if they were accepted as as a proposals, otherwise \(\beta_{0_1}\) and/or \(\beta_{0_1}\)
Repeat this entire process a pre=specified number of times. Eventually, the random draws should “converge” on a stable distribution that represents the posterior.

href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-i
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail I
In our example, where \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)
Step 1: Choose starting values for each parameter as draws from their prior distributions. Call them \(\beta_{0_1}\), \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).
Step 2: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{0}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{0_2}\).
Step 3: Determine whether \(\beta_{0_1}\) or \(\beta_{0_2}\) is at a higher point on the likelihood function (data given parameters), with \(\beta_{1}\) assumed to be \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) assumed to be \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).

That is: Check whether \(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail II
Step 4: If

\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\), keep the proposed value \(\beta_{0_2}\) for sure.
\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) < \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\) only keep \(\beta_{0_2}\) with probability based on the ratio \(\frac{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1}; \boldsymbol{D})}{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})}\)

Step 5: if \(\beta_{0_2}\) was kept, save it as a viable element of the posterior distribution of \(\beta_{0}\). Otherwise, throw it away.
Step 6: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{1}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{1_2}\).
Step 7: Repeat steps 3-5, but for \(\beta_{1_2}\) rather than \(\beta_{0_2}\), and using \(\beta_{0_2}\) if it was accepted as a proposal, and \(\beta_{0_1}\) if it was not.
Step 8: Repeat steps 3-5 for \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) using \(\beta_{0_2}\) and \(\beta_{1_2}\) if they were accepted as as a proposals, otherwise \(\beta_{0_1}\) and/or \(\beta_{0_1}\)
Repeat this entire process a pre=specified number of times. Eventually, the random draws should “converge” on a stable distribution that represents the posterior.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#section-8
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#section-8
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#point-estimates
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#point-estimates
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Point Estimates
The posterior distributions of each parameter can directly provide us inferential information.
Point estimates about parameters can be made using measures of central tendency

Mean: the posterior mean for a parameter is the value that will minimize squared error
Median: the posterior median for a parameter is the value that will minimize absolute error
Mode: “single” most likely parameter value

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Credible Intervals
The spread of the distributions quantify confidence in parameter estimates, or plausible values parameters might take

Posterior SDs are a measure of confidence
Credible intervals are everything we wish confidence intervals were

It is correct to say a we are 95% certain the population value falls within a 95% credible interval
This is based on the likelihood (data) and prior (existing knowledge and confidence).

Important: if our prior wasn’t true or was poorly chosen this result will not hold!
Prior should represent true report of one’s prior belief

Contrast this with our earlier definitions of frequentist confidence intervals!

In 95% of samples, true parameter will fall inside interval
Range of values we cannot reject if treated as null hypothesis

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#types-of-credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#types-of-credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Types of Credible Intervals
Equal Tailed Intervals (ETI):

Simply based on the symmetric quantiles of the distribution
E.g., for a 95% credible interval, 2.5% is outside in each of the upper and lower tails

Highest Posterior Density Intervals (HPD):

Proportion of the distribution such that all values outside of this range have less support than values inside
Not necessarily symmetrical in the tails

The two types will be equal in symmetric distributions, but will not be in asymmetric distributions. HPD is a better representation of the range best supported by the posterior (recommended)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#bayes-factors
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#bayes-factors
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors
Bayes Factors are a way of comparing the support for different models in a Bayesian framework.
They are ratios of posterior likelihoods between competing models. If we have two possible models for the same data, \(M_1\) and \(M_2\).
\[BF = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_1)}{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_2)}\]

When \(BF = 1\) the two models are equally likely
When \(BF > 1\) then \(M_1\) is more likely than \(M_2\)

When \(BF = 3\), \(M_1\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_2\)

When \(BF < 1\), \(M_2\) is more likely than \(M_1\)

When \(BF = \frac{1}{3}\), \(M_2\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_1\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#advantages-and-disadvantages
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#advantages-and-disadvantages
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Intuitive way to compare two (or more) models to one another
Fairly straightforward interpretation

Disadvantages:

Assume that the models being compared are THE models

No model is the “true” model!

Can lead to similar pitfalls as frequentist analysis

\(BF\) of 3 (or \(\frac{1}{3}\)) have been proposed as “cutoff” values. This is just as arbitrary as \(\alpha = .05\), and even sillier since Bayes Factors have a much more intuitive interpretation than \(p\)-values

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#bayes-factors-and-support-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#bayes-factors-and-support-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors and Support Intervals
Support Interval: Region of the posterior distribution of a parameter that is taller than the prior distribution.
Interpretation: Data added evidentiary support for this region over our prior.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#support-intervals
