objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#cross-validation
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#cross-validation
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Cross Validation
Cross validation (CV) methods slice data up into sections.
They use one part of data as a “training” sample, and another as a “testing” sample.
The downside to this is the loss of precision/power.
Leave one out (LOO) cross-validation takes all possible combinations of \(N-1\) observations, leaving one row out a time, and cross validates on that single observation.
Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling (PSIS) provides a method for estimating LOO-CV in a tractable way, and can be quite useful (though not always feasible).
This is a great method when available though, since models are validated on data that wasn’t in the sample on which they were fit, which is a huge bonus for generalizability and avoiding overfit.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#stan-and-rstanarm
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation.html#stan-and-rstanarm
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Stan and rstanarm

Stan is free general purpose, C++ based software for estimating Bayesian models

Uses “Hamiltonian” Monte Carlo

More sophisticated version of MCMC than Gibbs


rstanarm is a user friendly R package that implements several common statistical models in Stan using R syntax

Very smart default priors
Limited to specific set of common statistical models
We will only cover rstanarm

Slightly more advanced: brms
Even more advanced: cmdstanr and RStan

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#what-is-bayesian-inference
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#what-is-bayesian-inference
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
What is Bayesian Inference
NHST is a decision rule framework for how we make a categorical choice: do we decide to reject the null hypothesis?

Bayesian inference is also a kind of decision rule, but it is not discrete, it is continuous.
Way of defining how we can use new data to updating our existing beliefs about what a population parameter is likely to be.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
Let’s imagine we have a coin, we want to determine the true proportion of times that the coin will land on heads (vs. tails).

We will call the coin’s true proportion of landing on heads (which is unknown) \(\pi\).
We then flip the coin 10 times, and observe 7 heads and 3 tails, which is our “data,” which we will call \(\boldsymbol{D}\).

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
\[P(\theta|D) = \frac{P(D|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(D)}\]

\(P(\pi)\) - our prior belief about the proportion of times the coin will lands heads

Notice: The true \(\pi\) is unknown. This is a statement about our confidence it might take on certain values. So we might think it is very likely 50%, but there is some chance it is not, and is an unfair coin

\(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\) - The likelihood of observing 7 heads and 3 tails, given the (unknown) true \(\pi\).
\(P(\boldsymbol{D})\) - The probability of observing 7 heads and 3 tails unconditionally

One way to define this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\)
Really we typically need calculus for this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta\)

\(P(\theta | \boldsymbol{D})\) - the posterior belief about the proportion of times the coin will land on heads, incorporating both the prior and the data.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#probabilities-of-probabilities
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#probabilities-of-probabilities
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Probabilities of Probabilities
Notice that our prior is a probability statement about not about how likely the coin is to land on heads, but our confidence in the true proportion of times the coin will land on heads \(\pi\). If we are very confident, our prior might look something like this.

This plot suggests we think it’s very likely the coin is fair, though there’s some possibiliy is is weighted more heavily towards heads or tails.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#frequentists-hate-him
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#frequentists-hate-him
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Frequentists HATE him
This is the part frequentists object to. For a frequentist:

Only “random variables” can be represented by a probability distribution
The true proportion of heads is not a random variable
It is a single number, a cold hard fact, just one that we don’t know

For a Bayesian

Probability refers to what is known, not just what is true or not true

Bayseians treat probability as a psychological phenomenon
Frequentists treat probability as a metaphysical phenomenon

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#two-takes-on-probability
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#two-takes-on-probability
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Two Takes on Probability



Frequentists: Parameters are facts about the world that are constant and can only actually be single values. The only things that are random are the data. We can’t reverse the probability arrow population \(\rightarrow\) sample
Bayesians: The only constants we can actually know are the facts we observe (data). Based on our limited knowledge, we need to a way to quantify how likely different possible parameters are. Probability is a general use language we use to describe the likelihood of different unknowns (parameters) based on our knowledge (data)

Which philosophical position do you take?

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#posterior-belief
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Posterior Belief

If we have a strong prior belief, seeing 7 heads and 3 tails should make us think if our coin happens to be unfair, it’s more likely to be weighted towards heads than tails. But seven heads and three tails aren’t that surprising for a fair coin, so our belief won’t change that much.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#a-different-prior
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#a-different-prior
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
A Different Prior

What if an alien came to earth with no knowledge about how coins worked? They might have no idea the true proportion of times most coins land on heads, and think all possible values of \(\pi\) are equally likely

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#aliens-posterior-belief
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#aliens-posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Alien’s Posterior Belief

In this case, the data might be quite persuasive! After seeing 7 heads and 3 tails, the alien might be fairly convinced that the coin was weighted towards heads.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
In practice, priors are specified as probability distributions.
For example, if I am very confident the coin is likely to be fair, my prior might be a normal distribution with \(\mu = 0.5\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\).

\(\mu = 0.5\) means I think the true proportion of heads is most likely to be \(0.5\),
\(\sigma = 0.1\) means that in my mind, I am around 68% certain that the true proportion is between \(0.4\) and \(0.6\)

Because 68% of the values in a normal distribution are within 1 SD of the mean

Likewise, I am around 98% certain the true proportion is between \(0.3\) and \(0.7\)

Because 98% of the values in a normal distribution are within 2 SD of the mean

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
This prior would technically be improper. Can anyone see why?
A normal distribution can have values from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\), but a proportion can only be between 0 and 1
This is one of the reasons Bayesian Statsitics is more complex to learn.
You can use improper priors, but in general, proper priors are going to allow us to do more and more interesting things.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-incorportate-data
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#how-to-incorportate-data
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Incorportate Data
How does data move us from prior to posterior?
Through the likelihood function
\[P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)P(\pi)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\pi)\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#likelihood-function-of-our-data
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#likelihood-function-of-our-data
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text: Likelihood Function of our Data

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#maximum-likelihood
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#maximum-likelihood
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Maximum Likelihood
Recall: To find the maximum likelihood, we find the highest point on the hill

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#map-estimation
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#map-estimation
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MAP Estimation
One approach to Bayesian estimation is very similar to Maximum Likelihood. It is known as Maximum A Posteriori estimation (MAP). Under MAP, we aren’t necessarily interested in the actual probability distribution \(P(\pi |\boldsymbol{D})\), just the value of \(\pi\) that maximizes this function.
Notice what this allows us to do with Bayes’ rule:
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta}\]
Because we don’t care about the equality, only the maximum point, we can drop out the denominator, and instead say
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) \propto P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\]
Where \(\propto\) means “is proportional to”.
This is a common approach when the primary goal is making predictions, rather than making a confidence statement about parameter values.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#general-form
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#general-form
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Form
The coin flip was a motivating example, but not very practice. Our general version of Bayes’ rule is:
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})\)

This allows us to consider our confidence in multiple parameters simultaneously, represented generically as \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#general-linear-model
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#general-linear-model
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Linear Model
For example, recall that we can rewrite a \(t\)-test in the form of a simple linear model
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Group}_i + \epsilon_i\]
Our parameter space here is \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)

\(\beta_0 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 0\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 1\)
\(\sigma_\epsilon =\) shared standard deviation for each group (residual SD)

We want to estimate Bayes’ rule without losing the denominator, complex integral and all
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})  = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}}\]

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a simulation-based procedure for determining the goint of posterior distribution of all parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) when it’s too complicated to figure out numerically.
There are many different MCMC based algorithms. In a very general/intuitive sense, the way MCMC works is as follows:

We draw random values from \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) based on our prior, and check how well those values “fit” our likelihood
If the fit is not good enough we (might) throw away that draw (probabilistically) and make another one
If it is good enough, we keep it, and update our parameter estimates based on this value
We repeat this process many times, until we have a large “synthetic sample” of values that represent the combination of our prior and the likelihood
We use the simulated values that we kept as a representation of the posterior distribution \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-i
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-i
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail I
In our example, where \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)
Step 1: Choose starting values for each parameter as draws from their prior distributions. Call them \(\beta_{0_1}\), \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).
Step 2: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{0}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{0_2}\).
Step 3: Determine whether \(\beta_{0_1}\) or \(\beta_{0_2}\) is at a higher point on the likelihood function (data given parameters), with \(\beta_{1}\) assumed to be \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) assumed to be \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).

That is: Check whether \(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail II
Step 4: If

\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\), keep the proposed value \(\beta_{0_2}\) for sure.
\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) < \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\) only keep \(\beta_{0_2}\) with probability based on the ratio \(\frac{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1}; \boldsymbol{D})}{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})}\)

Step 5: if \(\beta_{0_2}\) was kept, save it as a viable element of the posterior distribution of \(\beta_{0}\). Otherwise, throw it away.
Step 6: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{1}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{1_2}\).
Step 7: Repeat steps 3-5, but for \(\beta_{1_2}\) rather than \(\beta_{0_2}\), and using \(\beta_{0_2}\) if it was accepted as a proposal, and \(\beta_{0_1}\) if it was not.
Step 8: Repeat steps 3-5 for \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) using \(\beta_{0_2}\) and \(\beta_{1_2}\) if they were accepted as as a proposals, otherwise \(\beta_{0_1}\) and/or \(\beta_{0_1}\)
Repeat this entire process a pre=specified number of times. Eventually, the random draws should “converge” on a stable distribution that represents the posterior.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#section-8
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#section-8

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#point-estimates
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#point-estimates
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Point Estimates
The posterior distributions of each parameter can directly provide us inferential information.
Point estimates about parameters can be made using measures of central tendency

Mean: the posterior mean for a parameter is the value that will minimize squared error
Median: the posterior median for a parameter is the value that will minimize absolute error
Mode: “single” most likely parameter value

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Credible Intervals
The spread of the distributions quantify confidence in parameter estimates, or plausible values parameters might take

Posterior SDs are a measure of confidence
Credible intervals are everything we wish confidence intervals were

It is correct to say a we are 95% certain the population value falls within a 95% credible interval
This is based on the likelihood (data) and prior (existing knowledge and confidence).

Important: if our prior wasn’t true or was poorly chosen this result will not hold!
Prior should represent true report of one’s prior belief

Contrast this with our earlier definitions of frequentist confidence intervals!

In 95% of samples, true parameter will fall inside interval
Range of values we cannot reject if treated as null hypothesis

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#types-of-credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#types-of-credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Types of Credible Intervals
Equal Tailed Intervals (ETI):

Simply based on the symmetric quantiles of the distribution
E.g., for a 95% credible interval, 2.5% is outside in each of the upper and lower tails

Highest Posterior Density Intervals (HPD):

Proportion of the distribution such that all values outside of this range have less support than values inside
Not necessarily symmetrical in the tails

The two types will be equal in symmetric distributions, but will not be in asymmetric distributions. HPD is a better representation of the range best supported by the posterior (recommended)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#bayes-factors
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#bayes-factors
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors
Bayes Factors are a way of comparing the support for different models in a Bayesian framework.
They are ratios of posterior likelihoods between competing models. If we have two possible models for the same data, \(M_1\) and \(M_2\).
\[BF = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_1)}{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_2)}\]

When \(BF = 1\) the two models are equally likely
When \(BF > 1\) then \(M_1\) is more likely than \(M_2\)

When \(BF = 3\), \(M_1\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_2\)

When \(BF < 1\), \(M_2\) is more likely than \(M_1\)

When \(BF = \frac{1}{3}\), \(M_2\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_1\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#advantages-and-disadvantages
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#advantages-and-disadvantages
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Intuitive way to compare two (or more) models to one another
Fairly straightforward interpretation

Disadvantages:

Assume that the models being compared are THE models

No model is the “true” model!

Can lead to similar pitfalls as frequentist analysis

\(BF\) of 3 (or \(\frac{1}{3}\)) have been proposed as “cutoff” values. This is just as arbitrary as \(\alpha = .05\), and even sillier since Bayes Factors have a much more intuitive interpretation than \(p\)-values

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#bayes-factors-and-support-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian Inference Estimation.html#bayes-factors-and-support-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors and Support Intervals
Support Interval: Region of the posterior distribution of a parameter that is taller than the prior distribution.
Interpretation: Data added evidentiary support for this region over our prior.

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Cross Validation
Cross validation (CV) methods slice data up into sections.
They use one part of data as a “training” sample, and another as a “testing” sample.
The downside to this is the loss of precision/power.
Leave one out (LOO) cross-validation takes all possible combinations of \(N-1\) observations, leaving one row out a time, and cross validates on that single observation.
Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling (PSIS) provides a method for estimating LOO-CV in a tractable way, and can be quite useful (though not always feasible).
This is a great method when available though, since models are validated on data that wasn’t in the sample on which they were fit, which is a huge bonus for generalizability and avoiding overfit.

The Lie Factor
Also proposed by Tufte
\[\text{lie factor} = \frac{\text{size of effect in graphic}}{\text{actual size of effect}}\]
Where, in our example

Size of effect in graphic: Difference in area between the two bars
Actual size of effect: Numerical difference between two bars

title: Lecture 3: Visualizing Data
text:
Principles of Axis Scaling

One of the most common mistakes I see in creating graphs

Software will often default to the range of values being graphed
Axis should represent a plausible range of values of data

If you are comparing multiple means, you often need to expand the axis range!

Reasonable heuristic: Use the observed range or IQR of values of a variable


Almost always important to think about on \(y\)-axis
Sometimes important to think about on \(x\)-axis
Don’t “zoom in” to exaggerate the size of an effect
Don’t “zoom out” to de-emphasize size of effect
Scale should be chosen such that it reasonably represents effect size

More on effect sizes later

Kernel function:

Two common options: normal and Epanechnikov
Epanechnikov kernel function is the most efficient method for kernel density plot

Width or Bandwidth:

A parameter that smooths the kernel density curve

Too much smoothing can lose too much information

Mean, SD, skewness, and kurtosis do not indicate modality

Bimodal distributions often have kurtosis < 0 (but not necessarily)

In addition to descriptive statistics, this one reason we always want to graph the distributions of variables

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Indepenent Trials

What if we want to know the probability we would get five pineapple bears from a bag of 10 (each bear has has \(\pi = .2\) of being pineapple)?

This is known as the binomial distribution
Two parameters, sample size (\(n\)) and probability of success (\(\pi\))
For any number of \(k\) successes

\[\begin{pmatrix} n \\ k\end{pmatrix}\pi^k (1-\pi)^{n-k}\]
Where
\[\begin{pmatrix} n \\ k\end{pmatrix} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Binomial Problems
The easiest way to do these problems “by hand” is to reduce the number of calculation steps.
For example, if I wanted to know the probability of nine or more pineapples, I would do
\[P(\text{nine or more pineapples}) = \frac{10!}{9!(10-9)!}.2^9 (1-.2)^{10-9} +\] \[\frac{10!}{10!(10-10)!}.2^10 (1-.2)^{10-10} = \text{some very small number}\]
Then to get fewer than nine
\[P(\text{fewer than nine pineapples}) = 1 - \text{that very small number}\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Problems
The easiest way to do these problems “by hand” is to reduce the number of calculation steps.
For example, if I wanted to know the probability of nine or more pineapples, I would do
\[P(\text{nine or more pineapples}) = \frac{10!}{9!(10-9)!}.2^9 (1-.2)^{10-9} +\] \[\frac{10!}{10!(10-10)!}.2^{10} (1-.2)^{10-10} = \text{some very small number}\]
Then to get fewer than nine
\[P(\text{fewer than nine pineapples}) = 1 - \text{that very small number}\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Poissons
You can also get cumulative probabilities from Poisson distributions. The cumulative probability of 11 or fewer calls in a given day would be
\[P(x \leq 11) = \sum_{i=0}^{11}\frac{e^{-8}8^{i}}{i!} = .89\]
And the probability of more than 11 calls would be
\[P(x > 11) = 1 - P(x \leq 11) = 1 - .89 = .11\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Visualizing Distributions
Two types of probability distributions

Probability mass functions (PMFs)

Appropriate for discrete variables
PMFs give the probability of a particular event
Think: bar plots (relative frequency on \(y\) axis)

Probability density functions (PDFs)

The probability of any specific event (technically) equals zero
PDFs give the relative probability of an event in the region

\(\rightarrow\) higher values in more likely regions

Think: histograms & kernel density plots (density on \(y\) axis)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Joint & Marginal
Joint probability: The probability of two events both occurring
\[P(A \cap B)\]

If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\)
If \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive, \(P(A \cap B) = 0\)

Marginal probability: The probability of one event occurring
\[P(A)\]

Irrespective of other events
\(P(A) = P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap \neg B)\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Probability and Statistics


Probability tells us how data are randomly generated based on some underlying facts about a population.

Numerical language for describing how likely different events are to occur
How we go from parameters \(\rightarrow\) data

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Terminology

Event: A possible outcome or combination of outcomes
Sample Space: All possible outcomes

Sample space for a coin flip is \(\text{\{heads, tails\}}\)

Curly brackets indicate a set of individual elements

Sample space for points in an NBA game \([0,\infty]\)

Square brackets indicate an inclusive interval

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Notation

\(P(A)\): The probability of event \(A\)
\(P(A \cap B)\): The probability of both event \(A\) and \(B\)
\(P(A \cap \neg B)\): The probability of both event \(A\) and NOT \(B\)
\(P(A \cup B)\): The probability of event \(A\) or \(B\)
\(P(A|B)\): The probability that event \(A\) happens given that event \(B\) has happened

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Axioms
Axiom (noun): 

Positivity: For any \(A\), \(0 \leq P(A) \leq 1\)
The sum of the probability of all elements of a sample space \(= 1\)

Example:

If I flip a coin, the probability of heads must be between 0 and 1, and the sum of the probability of heads and the probability of tails is always 1

Even for an unfair coin, one of the outcomes is guaranteed, and must happen if the other outcome does not happen

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Gummy Bears
Haribo Gold Bears come in 5 flavors:

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The “Classical” Definition of Probability
Suppose we have a bag of gummy bears with exactly equal numbers of the 5 flavors
If we randomly pick one gummy bear, what is the probability of picking a pineapple gummy?

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Bernoulli Trials
Drawing a pineapple gummy bear is known as a Bernoulli trial:

“Experiment” with exactly two possible outcomes
e.g., heads vs. tails, pass vs. fail this class, diagnosis vs. no diagnosis, pineapple vs. other flavor gummy

If we code a “success” as “1” and a “failure” as “0”, then the probability of success in any Bernoulli trial equals
\[\pi = \frac{\text{\# of ways to succeed}}{\text{\# of ways to succeed} + \text{\# of ways to fail}}\]
NOTE: \(\pi\) is generic notation for a parameter (population value) representing the probability of success, NOT 3.14159….

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Bernoulli Distribution

Remember that \(\pi\) is not a statistic but a parameter

Represents an underlying truth: the proportion of ways a success can happen out of how many ways successes and failures can both happen

If we imagine we were to start drawing gummy bears, we can define the outcomes as a probability distribution defined by the parameter \(\pi\)
\[\text{Pineapple Bear} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\]
Read: Pineapple bears are distributed Bernoulli (follow a Bernoulli distribution) with probability \(\pi\)
In the population, the Bernoulli distribution has

Mean \(\mu= \pi\)
Variance \(\sigma^2 = \pi(1-\pi)\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
More Bernoulli

Let’s code successes on a given trial \(i\) as \(y_i = \text{Pineapple Bear} = 1\) and \(\text{any other flavor} = 0\)
We can write the Bernoulli distribution as
\[P(y_i| \pi)=\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i}\]
That means, for \(y_i = \text{Pineapple Bear} = 1\)

\(\pi^{y_i} = \pi^{1} = \pi\)
\((1-\pi)^{1-y_i} = (1 - \pi)^{1 - 1} = 1\)
\(P(y_i| \pi)=\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i} = \pi(1) = \pi\)

And for \(y_i = \text{any other flavor} = 0\)

\(\pi^{y_i} = \pi^{0} = 1\)
\((1-\pi)^{1-y_i} = (1 - \pi)^{1 - 0} = (1 - \pi)\)
\(P(y_i| \pi)=\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i} = 1(1 - \pi) = 1 -\pi\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Alternate Bernoulli

You might also see it written this way:
\[P(y_i | \pi) = \pi(y_i) + (1 - \pi)(1 - y_i)\]
That means, for \(y_i = \text{Pineapple Bear} = 1\)

\(\pi(y_i) = \pi(1) = \pi\)
\((1 - \pi)(1 - y_i) = (1 \pi)(1 - 1) = 0\)
\(P(y_i| \pi) = \pi(y_i) + (1 - \pi)(1 - y_i) = \pi + 0 = \pi\)

And for \(y_i = \text{any other flavor} = 0\)

\(\pi(y_i) = \pi(0) = 0\)
\((1 - \pi)(1 - y_i) = (1 - \pi)(1 - 0) = 1 -\pi\)
\(P(y_i| \pi) = \pi(y_i) + (1 - \pi)(1 - y_i) = 0 + 1 -\pi = 1- \pi\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Multiple Trials

What if we sample more than one gummy bear?
Two ways:

Without replacement

Probability of a pineapple on the 2nd draw depends on the outcome of the first draw
Outcomes are dependent
The probability of an event changes depending on earlier events

With replacement

Probability of pineapple on the 2nd draw is the same as for the 1st draw
Outcomes are independent
The same probabilities apply to all events

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Indepenent Trials

What if we want to know the probability we would get five pineapple bears from a bag of 10 (each bear has has \(\pi = .2\) of being pineapple)?

This is known as the binomial distribution
Two parameters, sample size (\(n\)) and probability of success (\(\pi\))
For any number of \(k\) successes

\[\begin{pmatrix} n \\ k\end{pmatrix}\pi^k (1-\pi)^{n-k}\]
Where
\[\begin{pmatrix} n \\ k\end{pmatrix} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Binomial Distribution
What this means: If we repeatedly sampled bags of 10 gummy bears, we would expect to get exactly five pineapples with probability
\[P(\text{five pineapples}) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\pi^k (1-\pi)^{n-k} =\] \[\frac{10!}{5!(10-5)!}.2^5 (1-.2)^{10-5} = .026\]
For every 100 times we repeated this exercise, we would expect to get exactly five pineapples in 10 draws about three times.

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Binomial Distribution
We can write that variable \(X\) follows a binomial distribution with \(n\) draws and \(\pi\) probability of success on each draw as:
\[X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \pi)\]
In the population, the binomial distribution has

Mean \(\mu= n\pi\)
Variance \(\sigma^2 = n\pi(1-\pi)\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Binomials

We can also use the binomial distribution to consider cumulative outcomes by summing the probabilities of each outcome within a cumulative range.
For example, the probability that we would draw fewer than three (exactly zero, exactly one, or exactly two) pineapples in bags of 10 bears is:
\[P(\text{fewer than three pinapples}) = \frac{10!}{0!(10-0)!}.2^0 (1-.2)^{10-0} +\] \[\frac{10!}{1!(10-1)!}.2^1 (1-.2)^{10-1} + \frac{10!}{2!(10-2)!}.2^2 (1-.2)^{10-2} = .68\]
And we can get the complement of this cumulative probability by just subtracting it from 1. The probability we would draw at least three pineapples is
\[P(\text{at least three pinapples}) = 1 - P(\text{fewer than three pinapples}) =\] \[1 - .68 = .32\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Problems
The easiest way to do these problems “by hand” is to reduce the number of calculation steps.
For example, if I wanted to know the probability of nine or more pineapples, I would do
\[P(\text{nine or more pineapples}) = \frac{10!}{9!(10-9)!}.2^9 (1-.2)^{10-9} +\] \[\frac{10!}{10!(10-10)!}.2^{10} (1-.2)^{10-10} = \text{some very small number}\]
Then to get fewer than nine
\[P(\text{fewer than nine pineapples}) = 1 - \text{that very small number}\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Counting Events


The binomial distribution tells us the probability of a given number of successes in a fixed number of trials. Examples:

Number of pineapple gummies in a bag of 10
Number of heads in five coin flips

The Poisson distribution tells us how many “successes” occur (specific type of event happens) in a fixed time period. Examples:

Number of Ph.D. applications Georgia Tech receives in an application cycle
Number of calls a fire station gets on a given day


The difference between the binomial and Poisson

Binomial: Number of successes in a fixed number of trials
Poisson: Number of successes in unspecified number of trials over fixed time period

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Poisson Distribution
The Poisson distribution has the following form:
\[P(x) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}\]
Where

\(e\) is Euler’s number (base of natural logarithm) \(\approx 2.718\)
\(\mu\) is the mean number of successes in the population
\(x\) is the number of observed successes (or counts)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Poisson Example
If the mean number of calls to the fire station in a day is 8, the probability of getting exactly 11 calls in a given day would be
\[P(x = 11) = \frac{e^{-8}8^{11}}{11!} = .072\]
In the Poisson distribution

The population mean is \(\mu\)
The population variance \(\sigma^2\) also \(= \mu\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Cumulative Poissons
You can also get cumulative probabilities from Poisson distributions. The cumulative probability of 11 or fewer calls in a given day would be
\[P(x \leq 11) = \sum_{i=0}^{11}\frac{e^{-8}8^{i}}{i!} = .89\]
And the probability of more than 11 calls would be
\[P(x > 11) = 1 - P(x \leq 11) = 1 - .89 = .11\]

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Continuous Variables

The Bernoulli, Binomial, and Poisson distributions all involve discrete variables. What about continuous variables?

The Normal Distribution will be our major focus

Symmetrical with parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\)

The lognormal distribution: \(e^{\text{normal distribution}}\)

Creates distribution with lower boundary of zero and no upper boundary

The gamma distribution

A different distribution with a lower boundary of zero and no upper boundary

The beta distribution

Continuous distribution on the interval \([0, 1]\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Normal Distribution

The formula for the density of the normal distribution is
\[P(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}}e^{\frac{(-x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]
There are two parameters (here \(\pi\) is the number not a parameter!): \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). We can write that \(x\) is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) as
\[x \sim \text{normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)\]
Simple interpretation: In the population, the average value of \(x\) is \(\mu\) and the average amount of squared error between all members of the population and \(\mu\) is \(\sigma^2\)
Sometimes you will also see it as
\[x \sim \text{normal}(\mu, \sigma)\]
In which case we are referring to the standard deviation rather than the variance

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Normal Distribution Example
Let’s imagine in the population of all possible basketball players, the average player height is \(\mu = 200\)cm and the variance is \(\sigma^2 = 64\text{cm}^2\).
That means, if I randomly sampled a group of basketball players, I would expect:

The average height of players in my sample to be 200cm
The average squared difference between each players’ height and 200cm to be 64

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Visualizing Distributions
Two types of probability distributions

Probability mass functions (PMFs)

Appropriate for discrete variables
PMFs give the probability of a particular event
Think: bar plots (relative frequency on \(y\) axis)

Probability density functions (PDFs)

The probability of any specific event (technically) equals zero
PDFs give the relative probability of an event in the region

\(\rightarrow\) higher values in more likely regions

Think: histograms & kernel density plots (density on \(y\) axis)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Independence

Independent Events: The probability of one event happening does not depend on whether or not another event has happened
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent events:

\(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\)
\(P(A|B) = P(A)\)

Most statistical methods make use of the idea of independence

“Independence of observations” assumption
Assumes that if you know one data point and the parameters of the distribution, new data point doesn’t give you any new information about probability distribution of other data points

Non-independent: Knowing my height, how tall do you think my brother is?
Independent: Knowing my height, how tall do you think the next person to walk by the door will be?

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Joint & Marginal
Joint probability: The probability of two events both occurring
\[P(A \cap B)\]

If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\)
If \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive, \(P(A \cap B) = 0\)

Marginal probability: The probability of one event occurring
\[P(A)\]

Irrespective of other events
\(P(A) = P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap \neg B)\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Bayes’ Theorem

A better (more technical) definition of conditional probability:
\[P(A | B)  =   \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \vert A) P(A)}{P(B)}\]
This is known as Bayes’ Theorem
VERY IMPORTANT! In general:
\[P(A | B)  \neq    P(B | A)\]

\(P(\text{no cancer} \vert \text{positive test}) =\frac{\text{\# with no cancer and a positive test}}{\text{\# with a positive test}} = \frac{46}{140} = .33\)
\(P(\text{positive test} \vert \text{no cancer}) = \frac{\text{\# with no cancer and a positive test}}{\text{\# with cancer}} = \frac{46}{900} = .05\)

Which one of these do you think is more important to know when taking a diagnostic test? Which do you think is more likely to be known?

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
More Bayes’ Theorem
A better (more technical) definition of conditional probability:
\[P(A | B)  =   \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \vert A) P(A)}{P(B)}\]
This is known as Bayes’ Theorem
VERY IMPORTANT! In general:
\[P(A | B)  \neq    P(B | A)\]

\(P\)(guilty | evidence) \(\neq P\)(evidence | guilty)
\(P\)(data | hypothesis) \(\neq P\)(hypothesis | data)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Frequentist Approach
There are two predominant ways of doing statistical inference, and both rely heavily on probability theory.
Historically, the most popular is the frequentist approach:

Generate a hypothesis (or competing hypotheses) about parameters
Collect some data
Use what we know about probability to determine how (im)plausible our data are under the assumption they were governed by our hypothesized parameters

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
The Bayesian Approach
Less historically popular, but rapidly gaining momentum is the Bayesian approach

Start with a prior belief (probability distribution) over all different possible sets of parameters (\(\boldsymbol{\theta}\)): \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Look at how likely our data (\(\boldsymbol{D}\)) are under all different possible sets of parameters: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Use Bayes’ rule to revise our beliefs (probability distribution) about the parameters given the data we have observed: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
A Brief History of Bayesianism


Bayes theorem was first discovered by Reverend Thomas Bayes in 18th century

English Presbyterian Minister
Published defenses of science against religious claims science was heretical
Theorem didn’t make big waves until….

It was independently redisocvered by Pierre Simon Laplace

Gave much more formal mathematical definition
Later learned of Bayes and unselfishly gave Bayes credit for the discovery

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Bayes and Laplace




Thomas Bayes (1701-1761)


Pierre Simon Laplace (1749-1827)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
A Brief History of Frequentism


Post-enlightenment (early 20th century), there was strong desire for “objective” science
Bayesian inference requires subjectivity in the form of a prior belief
This was considered “perverse” by modern standards
Sir Ronald Fisher was one of the key backers of core philosophy behind contemporary frequentist statistics

Rejected Bayesianism
Highly prone to becoming polemic
Even had a very famous intellectual war with contemporary Jerzy Neyman over the “right” way to do frequentism

Even if Bayesianism was accepted, rigorous Bayesian inference required computational technology unavailable until the late 20th century

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
What is Bayesian Inference
NHST is a decision rule framework for how we make a categorical choice: do we decide to reject the null hypothesis?

Bayesian inference is also a kind of decision rule, but it is not discrete, it is continuous.
Way of defining how we can use new data to updating our existing beliefs about what a population parameter is likely to be.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#the-elements-of-bayes-rule
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
Let’s imagine we have a coin, we want to determine the true proportion of times that the coin will land on heads (vs. tails).

We will call the coin’s true proportion of landing on heads (which is unknown) \(\pi\).
We then flip the coin 10 times, and observe 7 heads and 3 tails, which is our “data,” which we will call \(\boldsymbol{D}\).

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
The Elements of Bayes’ Rule
\[P(\theta|D) = \frac{P(D|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(D)}\]

\(P(\pi)\) - our prior belief about the proportion of times the coin will lands heads

Notice: The true \(\pi\) is unknown. This is a statement about our confidence it might take on certain values. So we might think it is very likely 50%, but there is some chance it is not, and is an unfair coin

\(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\) - The likelihood of observing 7 heads and 3 tails, given the (unknown) true \(\pi\).
\(P(\boldsymbol{D})\) - The probability of observing 7 heads and 3 tails unconditionally

One way to define this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\)
Really we typically need calculus for this: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}) = \int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta\)

\(P(\theta | \boldsymbol{D})\) - the posterior belief about the proportion of times the coin will land on heads, incorporating both the prior and the data.

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Probabilities of Probabilities
Notice that our prior is a probability statement about not about how likely the coin is to land on heads, but our confidence in the true proportion of times the coin will land on heads \(\pi\). If we are very confident, our prior might look something like this.

This plot suggests we think it’s very likely the coin is fair, though there’s some possibiliy is is weighted more heavily towards heads or tails.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#frequentists-hate-him
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#frequentists-hate-him
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Frequentists HATE him
This is the part frequentists object to. For a frequentist:

Only “random variables” can be represented by a probability distribution
The true proportion of heads is not a random variable
It is a single number, a cold hard fact, just one that we don’t know

For a Bayesian

Probability refers to what is known, not just what is true or not true

Bayseians treat probability as a psychological phenomenon
Frequentists treat probability as a metaphysical phenomenon

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#two-takes-on-probability
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#two-takes-on-probability
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Two Takes on Probability



Frequentists: Parameters are facts about the world that are constant and can only actually be single values. The only things that are random are the data. We can’t reverse the probability arrow population \(\rightarrow\) sample
Bayesians: The only constants we can actually know are the facts we observe (data). Based on our limited knowledge, we need to a way to quantify how likely different possible parameters are. Probability is a general use language we use to describe the likelihood of different unknowns (parameters) based on our knowledge (data)

Which philosophical position do you take?

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#posterior-belief
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Posterior Belief

If we have a strong prior belief, seeing 7 heads and 3 tails should make us think if our coin happens to be unfair, it’s more likely to be weighted towards heads than tails. But seven heads and three tails aren’t that surprising for a fair coin, so our belief won’t change that much.

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
A Different Prior

What if an alien came to earth with no knowledge about how coins worked? They might have no idea the true proportion of times most coins land on heads, and think all possible values of \(\pi\) are equally likely

href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#aliens-posterior-belief
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Alien’s Posterior Belief

In this case, the data might be quite persuasive! After seeing 7 heads and 3 tails, the alien might be fairly convinced that the coin was weighted towards heads.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-specify-your-prior
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
In practice, priors are specified as probability distributions.
For example, if I am very confident the coin is likely to be fair, my prior might be a normal distribution with \(\mu = 0.5\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\).

\(\mu = 0.5\) means I think the true proportion of heads is most likely to be \(0.5\),
\(\sigma = 0.1\) means that in my mind, I am around 68% certain that the true proportion is between \(0.4\) and \(0.6\)

Because 68% of the values in a normal distribution are within 1 SD of the mean

Likewise, I am around 98% certain the true proportion is between \(0.3\) and \(0.7\)

Because 98% of the values in a normal distribution are within 2 SD of the mean

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-specify-your-prior-1
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Specify your Prior
This prior would technically be improper. Can anyone see why?
A normal distribution can have values from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\), but a proportion can only be between 0 and 1
This is one of the reasons Bayesian Statsitics is more complex to learn.
You can use improper priors, but in general, proper priors are going to allow us to do more and more interesting things.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-incorportate-data
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#how-to-incorportate-data
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
How to Incorportate Data
How does data move us from prior to posterior?
Through the likelihood function
\[P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)P(\pi)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\pi)\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\pi)\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\pi|\boldsymbol{D})\)

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text: Likelihood Function of our Data

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#maximum-likelihood
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#maximum-likelihood
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Maximum Likelihood
Recall: To find the maximum likelihood, we find the highest point on the hill

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#map-estimation
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#map-estimation
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MAP Estimation
One approach to Bayesian estimation is very similar to Maximum Likelihood. It is known as Maximum A Posteriori estimation (MAP). Under MAP, we aren’t necessarily interested in the actual probability distribution \(P(\pi |\boldsymbol{D})\), just the value of \(\pi\) that maximizes this function.
Notice what this allows us to do with Bayes’ rule:
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta}\]
Because we don’t care about the equality, only the maximum point, we can drop out the denominator, and instead say
\[P(\theta|\boldsymbol{D}) \propto P(\boldsymbol{D}|\theta)P(\theta)\]
Where \(\propto\) means “is proportional to”.
This is a common approach when the primary goal is making predictions, rather than making a confidence statement about parameter values.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#general-form
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#general-form
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Form
The coin flip was a motivating example, but not very practice. Our general version of Bayes’ rule is:
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D}) = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})}\]

Prior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Likelihood: \(P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\)
Scaling term: \(P(\boldsymbol{D})\)
Posterior: \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})\)

This allows us to consider our confidence in multiple parameters simultaneously, represented generically as \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#general-linear-model
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#general-linear-model
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
General Linear Model
For example, recall that we can rewrite a \(t\)-test in the form of a simple linear model
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Group}_i + \epsilon_i\]
Our parameter space here is \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)

\(\beta_0 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 0\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1 =\) sample mean when \(\text{Group}_i = 1\)
\(\sigma_\epsilon =\) shared standard deviation for each group (residual SD)

We want to estimate Bayes’ rule without losing the denominator, complex integral and all
\[P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\boldsymbol{D})  = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{P(\boldsymbol{D})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\sum P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})} = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int P(\boldsymbol{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})P(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}}\]

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#markov-chain-monte-carlo
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a simulation-based procedure for determining the goint of posterior distribution of all parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) when it’s too complicated to figure out numerically.
There are many different MCMC based algorithms. In a very general/intuitive sense, the way MCMC works is as follows:

We draw random values from \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) based on our prior, and check how well those values “fit” our likelihood
If the fit is not good enough we (might) throw away that draw (probabilistically) and make another one
If it is good enough, we keep it, and update our parameter estimates based on this value
We repeat this process many times, until we have a large “synthetic sample” of values that represent the combination of our prior and the likelihood
We use the simulated values that we kept as a representation of the posterior distribution \(P(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \boldsymbol{D})\)

href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#mcmc-more-detail-i
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail I
In our example, where \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma_\epsilon]\)
Step 1: Choose starting values for each parameter as draws from their prior distributions. Call them \(\beta_{0_1}\), \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).
Step 2: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{0}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{0_2}\).
Step 3: Determine whether \(\beta_{0_1}\) or \(\beta_{0_2}\) is at a higher point on the likelihood function (data given parameters), with \(\beta_{1}\) assumed to be \(\beta_{1_1}\) and \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) assumed to be \(\sigma_{\epsilon_1}\).

That is: Check whether \(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#mcmc-more-detail-ii
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
MCMC: More Detail II
Step 4: If

\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\), keep the proposed value \(\beta_{0_2}\) for sure.
\(\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D}) < \mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})\) only keep \(\beta_{0_2}\) with probability based on the ratio \(\frac{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_2}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1}; \boldsymbol{D})}{\mathcal{L}(\beta_{0_1}, \beta_{1_1}, \sigma_{\epsilon_1} ; \boldsymbol{D})}\)

Step 5: if \(\beta_{0_2}\) was kept, save it as a viable element of the posterior distribution of \(\beta_{0}\). Otherwise, throw it away.
Step 6: Draw a new random value for \(\beta_{1}\) from its prior distribution. Call this \(\beta_{1_2}\).
Step 7: Repeat steps 3-5, but for \(\beta_{1_2}\) rather than \(\beta_{0_2}\), and using \(\beta_{0_2}\) if it was accepted as a proposal, and \(\beta_{0_1}\) if it was not.
Step 8: Repeat steps 3-5 for \(\sigma_{\epsilon}\) using \(\beta_{0_2}\) and \(\beta_{1_2}\) if they were accepted as as a proposals, otherwise \(\beta_{0_1}\) and/or \(\beta_{0_1}\)
Repeat this entire process a pre=specified number of times. Eventually, the random draws should “converge” on a stable distribution that represents the posterior.

href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#point-estimates
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Point Estimates
The posterior distributions of each parameter can directly provide us inferential information.
Point estimates about parameters can be made using measures of central tendency

Mean: the posterior mean for a parameter is the value that will minimize squared error
Median: the posterior median for a parameter is the value that will minimize absolute error
Mode: “single” most likely parameter value

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Credible Intervals
The spread of the distributions quantify confidence in parameter estimates, or plausible values parameters might take

Posterior SDs are a measure of confidence
Credible intervals are everything we wish confidence intervals were

It is correct to say a we are 95% certain the population value falls within a 95% credible interval
This is based on the likelihood (data) and prior (existing knowledge and confidence).

Important: if our prior wasn’t true or was poorly chosen this result will not hold!
Prior should represent true report of one’s prior belief

Contrast this with our earlier definitions of frequentist confidence intervals!

In 95% of samples, true parameter will fall inside interval
Range of values we cannot reject if treated as null hypothesis

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#types-of-credible-intervals
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#types-of-credible-intervals
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Types of Credible Intervals
Equal Tailed Intervals (ETI):

Simply based on the symmetric quantiles of the distribution
E.g., for a 95% credible interval, 2.5% is outside in each of the upper and lower tails

Highest Posterior Density Intervals (HPD):

Proportion of the distribution such that all values outside of this range have less support than values inside
Not necessarily symmetrical in the tails

The two types will be equal in symmetric distributions, but will not be in asymmetric distributions. HPD is a better representation of the range best supported by the posterior (recommended)

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#bayes-factors
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#bayes-factors
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors
Bayes Factors are a way of comparing the support for different models in a Bayesian framework.
They are ratios of posterior likelihoods between competing models. If we have two possible models for the same data, \(M_1\) and \(M_2\).
\[BF = \frac{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_1)}{P(\boldsymbol{D}|M_2)}\]

When \(BF = 1\) the two models are equally likely
When \(BF > 1\) then \(M_1\) is more likely than \(M_2\)

When \(BF = 3\), \(M_1\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_2\)

When \(BF < 1\), \(M_2\) is more likely than \(M_1\)

When \(BF = \frac{1}{3}\), \(M_2\) is three times as likely to be the “true” model as \(M_1\)

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Intuitive way to compare two (or more) models to one another
Fairly straightforward interpretation

Disadvantages:

Assume that the models being compared are THE models

No model is the “true” model!

Can lead to similar pitfalls as frequentist analysis

\(BF\) of 3 (or \(\frac{1}{3}\)) have been proposed as “cutoff” values. This is just as arbitrary as \(\alpha = .05\), and even sillier since Bayes Factors have a much more intuitive interpretation than \(p\)-values

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Bayes Factors and Support Intervals
Support Interval: Region of the posterior distribution of a parameter that is taller than the prior distribution.
Interpretation: Data added evidentiary support for this region over our prior.

objectID: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#cross-validation
href: lecture/slides/15 Bayesian Inference and Estimation/Lecture 15 Bayesian.html#cross-validation
title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Cross Validation
Cross validation (CV) methods slice data up into sections.
They use one part of data as a “training” sample, and another as a “testing” sample.
The downside to this is the loss of precision/power.
Leave one out (LOO) cross-validation takes all possible combinations of \(N-1\) observations, leaving one row out a time, and cross validates on that single observation.
Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling (PSIS) provides a method for estimating LOO-CV in a tractable way, and can be quite useful (though not always feasible).
This is a great method when available though, since models are validated on data that wasn’t in the sample on which they were fit, which is a huge bonus for generalizability and avoiding overfit.

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Stan and rstanarm

Stan is free general purpose, C++ based software for estimating Bayesian models

Uses “Hamiltonian” Monte Carlo

More sophisticated version of MCMC than Gibbs


rstanarm is a user friendly R package that implements several common statistical models in Stan using R syntax

Very smart default priors
Limited to specific set of common statistical models
We will only cover rstanarm

Slightly more advanced: brms
Even more advanced: cmdstanr and RStan

title: Lecture 15: Bayesian Inference and Estimation
text:
Priors
By default, rstanarm uses the following priors

For \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) the prior is based on a normal distribution with \(\sigma = 2.5\)

\(\sigma = 2.5\) is based on a transformed scale, using information about the variables in the model to convert to \(z\)-score units
The intercept \(\beta_0\) has \(\mu\) based on the overall mean
The slope \(\beta_1\) has \(\mu = 0\)

\(\sigma\) is given a prior based on an exponential distribution

Non-negative distribution, also scaled to \(z\)-score-like units



prior_summary(stan_lm1)

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Data Types Interlude: Factors
New data type (to us): factor variable: a built-in data type that R provides for categorical variables
Sets fixed possibilities of values that the variable can take on


If you have a variable with days of the week…

days <- c("Tues", "Wed", "Thurs")

Nothing preventing typos and no sensible sorting

moredays <- c("Teus", "Wed", "Thrus")
sort(days)

[1] "Thurs" "Tues"  "Wed"  



Factors help with both. Start by creating a vector of levels. Can also make labels for nicer printing.

weekday_levels <- c("Mon", "Tues", "Wed", "Thurs", "Fri")
weekday_labels <- c("Mon" = "Monday", 
                    "Tues" = "Tuesday", 
                    "Wed" = "Wednesday", 
                    "Thurs" = "Thursday", 
                    "Fri" = "Friday")

And now make a factor

days_fct <- factor(days, levels = weekday_levels, 
                   labels = weekday_labels)

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Transform: Factor Variables
Will convert to NA if not valid level

factor(moredays, levels = weekday_levels)

[1] <NA> Wed  <NA>
Levels: Mon Tues Wed Thurs Fri


Better sorting

sort(days_fct)

[1] Tuesday   Wednesday Thursday 
Levels: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday

text:

Within a dataframe, we can modify or create columns by pulling the column out with $ and assigning it to something new.

position_levels <- c("GK", "DEF", "MID", "FWD")
position_labels <- c("GK" = "Goalkeeper",
                     "DEF" = "Defense",
                     "MID" = "Midfield",
                     "FWD" = "Forward")


player_stats$position_fct <- factor(player_stats$position,
                                    levels = position_levels,
                                    labels = position_labels)
player_stats$position_fct |> head()

[1] Goalkeeper Defense    Defense    Defense    Defense    Midfield  
Levels: Goalkeeper Defense Midfield Forward

text:
Visualize (Bonus!)
If you’d like more practice doing data visualization, here are some extra exercises. These will not count towards your grade, but I will provide feedback if you choose to do them for practice.

B1) Let’s plot the billboards data. Let’s make a line graph that has time (week) on the x-axis and a song’s ranking on the y-axis. Start by using the ggplot() function to make a grid with axes (no geoms yet).

billboard_l |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = ranking))










B2) Now, let’s add a geom_line() to show the rankings of the different songs over time. Remember you will need to add a group argument to your aes.

billboard_l |>

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit: Hypotheses
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit: Hypotheses
\(H_0\): Observed data match the expected frequencies for the population
\(H_1\): Observed data do not match the expected frequencies for the population
○ Observed frequency is significantly different than expected

\(H_0\): \(\pi_j = \pi_{j_0}\) for all categories \(j\) (i.e., difference for all categories is 0), where
\(\pi_j\) = observed proportion
\(\pi_{j_0}\) = expected proportion
\(H_1\): \(\pi_j \neq \pi_{j_0}\) for any category \(j\)

title: Chi-Squared and T-Tests
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]
where
\(O_j\) = observed frequency
\(N\) = total sample size
\(E_j\) = expected frequency
\(j\) = individual category out of \(J\) total categories
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each group.

title: Chi-Squared and T-Tests
section: \(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit Generally
\(\text{df} = J - 1\), where
\(J\) = number of categories
Use to identify critical \(\chi^2\) value from \(\chi^2\) table, R, etc.
For \(\chi^2\), as \(\text{df}\) increases, so does the critical-\(\chi^2\) value (at same \(\alpha\))
Only ever a one-tailed test! For the upper end of the distribution.

\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence
Do the observed frequencies of a categorical variable differ from what expected via properties of independence?
○ Now considering more than one type of category
○ E.g., Number of pets by cat vs. dog people and undergrad vs. post-graduate




Cat Person
Dog Person



Undergrad




Post-Graduate






Expected frequencies calculated from the marginal totals of the contingency table
○ Expected values determined from data

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence: Hypotheses
\(H_0\): Categorical Variable 1 and Categorical Variable 2 are independent (i.e., have no association)
\(H_1\): Categorical Variable 1 and Categorical Variable 2 are not independent (i.e., have some association)
○ Do expected frequencies match those expected via independence?

Mathematically the same as before:
\(H_0\): \(\pi_j = \pi_{j_0}\) for all categories \(j\); difference for all categories is 0, where
\(\pi_j\) = observed proportion
\(\pi_{j_0}\) = expected proportion
\(H_1\): \(\pi_j \neq \pi_{j_0}\) for any category \(j\)


Just changing the expected frequencies

title: Chi-Squared and T-Tests
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence Generally
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]
Basically identical formula to calculate the \(\chi^2\).
The difference is that our expected frequencies \(E_j\) are derived from the data. Just like before, we calculate the difference from each cell, but now we have two categories that make up the cell.
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each cell.

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]
where
\(O_j\) = observed frequency
\(N\) = total sample size
\(E_j\) = expected frequency
\(j\) = individual category out of \(J\) total categories
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each group.

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
\(\chi^2\) Test of Goodness of Fit
\(\text{df} = J - 1\), where
\(J\) = number of categories
Use to identify critical \(\chi^2\) value from \(\chi^2\) table, R, etc.
For \(\chi^2\), as \(\text{df}\) increases, so does the critical-\(\chi^2\) value (at same \(\alpha\))
Only ever a one-tailed test! For the upper end of the distribution.

\(\chi^2\) Test of Independence
\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – N\pi_{j_0})^2}{N\pi_{j_0}} = \sum_{j_1=1}^{J_1}\sum_{j_2=1}^{J_2} \frac{(O_j – E_j)^2}{E_j} \]

The difference is that our expected frequencies \(E_j\) are derived from the data. Just like before, we calculate the difference from each cell, but now we have two categories that make up the cell.
The sum of the squared differences between the observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequency, for each cell.

text:
T-Statistic Cutoffs
Say you want to find the cutoff t values: \(t(\text{df}=3)\) and \(t(\text{df}=37)\) for \(\alpha = .05\), both upper one-tailed and two-tailed.

Which will have the larger magnitude cutoff values?



One-Tailed
All of our \(\alpha = .05\) goes on the upper side
Need a cutoff for \(.95\)

qt(p = .95, df = 3)

[1] 2.353363

qt(p = .05, df = 37, lower.tail = F)

[1] 1.687094


\(t_{crit}(\text{df}=3) = 2.35\)
\(t_{crit}(\text{df}=37) = 1.69\)

Two-Tailed
\(\alpha = 1 - .95 = 5\%\) on both sides
So \(.05 / 2 = .025\) on each side
Need value for \(.025\) and \(.95 + .025\) (\([.025, .975]\))

qt(p = c(.025, .975), df = 3)

[1] -3.182446  3.182446

qt(p = c(.025, .975), df = 37)

[1] -2.026192  2.026192


\(t_{crit}(\text{df}=3) = [-3.18, 3.18]\)
\(t_{crit}(\text{df}=37) = [-2.03, 2.03]\)

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Independent Sample T-Test
Might want to compare two samples of observations
○ Post-graduation salaries of GT vs. UGA grads
○ Treatment vs. control group
○ Cats vs. dogs
We can represent each group with their mean on some outcome and compare the means
Consider whether the mean difference is significant but also have to account for different levels of variability within group

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Independent Sample T-Test: Pooled SD
Need to pool the sample SDs while noting different sample sizes
\[ s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2}{(n_1 - 1) + (n_2 - 1)} = \frac{(n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Independent Sample T-Test: Pooled SD
Note that when sample size is equal (i.e., \(n_1 = n_2 = n\)),

\[\begin{array}{ll}
  s_p^2 \bigg|_{n_1 = n_2 = n} & = \frac{(n - 1) s_1^2 + (n - 1) s_2^2}{(n - 1) + (n - 1)} = \frac{(n - 1) (s_1^2 + s_2^2)}{(n - 1) + (n - 1)} \\[0.6em]
   & = \frac{(n - 1) (s_1^2 + s_2^2)}{2(n - 1)} = \frac{s_1^2 + s_2^2}{2}
\end{array}\]


Square root to get back to standard deviation
\[ s_p = \sqrt{s_p^2} = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2}{(n_1 - 1) + (n_2 - 1)}} = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}} \]

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Independent Sample T-Test: Test statistic
\[ t = \frac{\bar{x_1} - \bar{x_2}}{\sqrt{\frac{s_p^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_p^2}{n_2}}} = \frac{\bar{x_1} - \bar{x_2}}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]
Compare against critical t-value with df = \((n_1 - 1) + (n_2 - 2)\)

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Paired Sample T-Test
Comparing the same subjects under two conditions (typically two timepoints)
○ Stress levels before vs. after a test
○ Reaction times before vs. after caffiene consumption
○ Anxiety levels before vs. after a mindfulness intervention
We can still use the mean to represent the observations in each condition and make comparisons
This time, focus on difference scores (individual differences in the observations between the two conditions)

title: Chi-Squared Tests, T-Tests, Effect Size
text:
Paired Sample T-Test
Need difference score for each observation \(d_i = x_2 - x_1\)
Then, get mean difference \(\bar{d} = \frac{d_1+d_2+...+d_n}{n}\) and standard deviation of those difference scores \(s_d = \sqrt{\frac{(d_1-\bar{d})^2 + (d_2-\bar{d})^2 + ... + (d_n-\bar{d})^2}{n - 1}}\)
\[ t = \frac{\bar{d} - \mu_{d_0}}{\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}} = \text{(usually)} \frac{\bar{d} - 0}{\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}} = \frac{\bar{d}}{\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}}\]
Compare against critical t-value with df = \(n - 1\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
What is More Likely?

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU})\) or \(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cap \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\)

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU})\) includes all the times Georgia Tech wins and scores less than 20

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cap \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\) or \(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cup \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\)

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cup \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\) includes all the times Georgia Tech wins and scores less than 20 AND includes all the times Georgia Tech loses while scoring at least 20

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cap \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\) or \(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} | \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\)

\(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} \cap \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\) includes cases where both must me true out of ALL cases, while \(P(\text{Georgia Tech Beats CU} | \text{Georgia Tech Scores at least 20})\) only considers cases where Georgia Tech scores at least 20 (smaller denominoator)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Practice
Lets say DoorDash orders come within the estimated delivery time 85% of the time. If you make five DoorDash orders, what is the probability that fewer than four will come within the estimated delivery window?
Easier to first calculate four or more, then subtract that from 1
\(P(\text{four or more on time}) = \frac{5!}{4!(5-4)!}.85^4 (1-.85)^{5-4} +\) \(\frac{5!}{5!(5-5)!}.85^5 (1-.85)^{5-5} = .84\)
\(P(\text{fewer than four on time}) = 1 - .84 = .16\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Practice
You work at a car dealership that sells on average three cars in a given week. What is the probability you sell one or fewer cars in a given week?
\(P(x \leq 1) = \frac{e^{-3}3^{0}}{0!} +\frac{e^{-3}3^{1}}{1!}  = .20\)
What is the probability you sell more than one car in a given week?
\(P(x > 1) = 1 - .20 = .80\)

title: Lecture 4: Probability
text:
Review

How are PMFs and PDFs different?

PMFs give exact probabilities of discrete events. PDFs give densities representing the relative probabilities of continuous events within given ranges

How are PMFs different from the bar plots we discussed last time?

PMFs represent the discrete probability distribution for the population while bar plots represent the empirical distribution of the sample

How are PDFs different from the kernel density plots we discussed last time?

PDFs represent the continuous probability distribution for the population while kernel density plots represent the empirical distribution of the sample
